name: fig4-nonresponder-dynamics
title: Fig 4 — responder vs non-responder dynamics
question: Under a single fixed multi-stage intervention, does the in-silico population split into responders (heal) and non-responders (still die), and do the non-responders show the paper's hallmark — a hyper-productive GCSF/neutrophil response that compounds inflammation?
experiment: Run 40 replicates untreated and 40 under the digitized Fig-2 intervention. Split the treated runs into responders / non-responders and compare the responder-average vs a representative non-responder for oxygen deficit, total GCSF, and neutrophil population. Reproduces Fig 4A-C.

behavior_tests.name: responders-and-nonresponders
behavior_tests.description: The fixed intervention lowers mortality below baseline yet leaves a nonzero population of non-responders (patients who still die under treatment). Pass if at least one non-responder exists.

visualizations.name: nonresponder-dynamics
visualizations.description: Three panels (oxygen deficit, total GCSF, neutrophil population) overlaying the responder average (blue) and a non-responder (red) — reproduction of Fig 4.

report.verdict: Non-responder phenomenon reproduced (population splits 5 responders / 35 non-responders). The digitized intervention itself is not beneficial at the population level — a digitization/approximation limitation, not a failure of the model — so this study supports the non-responder claim but not a mortality reduction from the digitized genome.

result: 5 responders, 35 non-responders (primary test n_nonresponders > 0 PASSES); treated 88% vs baseline 80% mortality.
